questions.q: The balance check on region gives p = 0.028, though the randomization was done by shuffling labels. What is the best response?
options: Discard the experiment
Treat it as chance, run a sensitivity check (does the effect look the same within each region?), note it, and move on
Add region as the new primary metric
Re-randomize until the p-value exceeds 0.05
questions.explain: With random assignment any imbalance is chance, and small p-values appear occasionally when you run several balance checks. A within-region check showed the same direction in every region.

questions.q: Churn was 22.36% in control and 19.56% in treatment, with a 95% CI for the difference of -5.06 to -0.54 points. What is the best summary?
options: Treatment cut churn by exactly 2.8 points
The reduction is between 5.06 and 0.54 points with certainty
Churn probably fell, by about 2.8 points, but the true reduction could be quite small
There is no evidence of any effect
questions.explain: The interval excludes zero, supporting a real reduction, but it is wide, so the size of the reduction is uncertain.

questions.q: The plan applies a Bonferroni correction for two outcomes. Churn has p = 0.015 and spend has p = 0.88. Which conclusion follows?
options: Neither outcome is significant
Both outcomes are significant
Only spend is significant
Churn passes the 0.025 threshold; spend does not
questions.explain: Bonferroni threshold is 0.05 / 2 = 0.025. 0.015 is below it and 0.88 is not.

questions.q: Why did the analysis pair a Welch t-test on spend with a bootstrap interval and a look at the medians?
options: Spend is right-skewed, so extra checks add robustness beyond a comparison of means
Bootstrapping always gives smaller p-values
Medians are required for any t-test
Spend has missing values
questions.explain: The skew of 2.61 and mean above median signal a long right tail, so a bootstrap and the medians provide a robustness check on the mean-based result.

questions.q: The regression of spend on prior sessions has slope 3.60 and R-squared of 0.053. How should you describe it?
options: Prior sessions cause a $3.60 increase in spend, and explain 5.3% of the variation
Each extra prior session is associated with about $3.60 more spend, but explains only about 5% of the variation, and this is not proof of cause
Prior sessions explain 94.7% of the variation in spend
The slope is meaningless because R-squared is small
questions.explain: The slope is a real association, but low R-squared means most variation is unexplained, and observational data does not prove that increasing sessions would raise spend.
